name: Dunkin’ self-ordering
label: UI design · Service concept
headline: A coffee order, comfortably within reach.
description: A tabletop ordering concept connecting the physical dining experience with a clear digital flow.
scope: Tabletop interaction, menu, order summary, payment
sections: A self-ordering tablet positioned at the table lets customers place an order without leaving their seats. The concept considers both screen navigation and the physical position of the device.
An interface that meets the customer

The proposed tablet adjusts to a comfortable angle when a button is pressed and rotates to serve people across the table. The physical interaction is part of the service concept, rather than a built or validated hardware product.

The screens connect a welcome page, product categories, a menu, an order summary, payment selection, and a successful-order confirmation. Orange and pink carry the brand’s familiar visual character through the journey.
A clear finish to the order
The payment screen presents the available methods, followed by an order confirmation. These final touchpoints help communicate what happens next after a customer has selected their items.
outcome: A connected set of interface concepts for tabletop ordering. The portfolio documents the proposed device interaction and screen flow; it does not report a deployed system or measured usability results.

name: Divine Dried Delicacies
label: Packaging · Structural design
headline: A gift box with a second life.
description: Four fold-out compartments turn a compact dry-fruit gift box into a serving tray.
scope: Research, structure, dielines, prototypes, visual design
sections: Make gifting useful beyond the moment
The aim was to create a multifunctional gift box that also works as a display tray. The design brings together presentation, portability, and the practical experience of serving dry fruits.

Research looked at premium dried-fruit brands, luxury gifting, and modular packaging. Four compartments fold outward for serving and return inward to make a compact box. An integrated handle supports carrying.
Testing how the structure comes together

The project used paperboard for a lightweight but sturdy structure. Dielines and physical iterations explored the folding mechanism and compartment stability. Purple and gold motifs gave the packaging a celebratory identity.
outcome: One package, two functions: the four-compartment gift box opens into a serving tray and folds back for storage. Dielines and physical prototypes demonstrate the transformation and the integrated carrying handle. This changes the package’s intended use beyond gifting; durability, waste reduction, and user satisfaction were not measured.
outcome_heading: From gift box to a reusable serving format.

name: Eclectics magazine
label: Editorial · Magazine design
headline: Giving fashion a rhythm on the page.
description: A fashion magazine exploration balancing photography, expressive headlines, and a three-column grid.
sections: A grid with room for expression
The magazine uses a three-column grid as the primary organizing structure. Within it, larger photographs, headlines, and smaller reading blocks create different levels of visual emphasis.
The sequence moves between image-led layouts and denser editorial pages. The project explores how alignment, scale, and color can hold varied fashion content together.
outcome: A magazine cover and collection of editorial spreads demonstrating grid-based layout and visual hierarchy.

name: Busan, in print
label: Editorial · Coffee-table book
headline: A city, explored one spread at a time.
description: A photography-led coffee-table book about Busan’s culture, coastline, food, and everyday experiences.
scope: Book cover, contents, image and text layouts
sections: The book presents Busan as a place to discover through its landscapes and culture. Large photographs and an airy title treatment establish the visual direction, with supporting text adding context.
The spreads cover themes including festivals, beaches, temples, and food. The page system combines photography and short text blocks to build a varied but connected reading experience.
outcome: A coffee-table book design with a cover, contents, and thematic spreads that organize a city narrative through photography and typography.

name: Conflictorium
label: Environmental graphics · Installation
headline: One installation. More than one perspective.
description: An environmental-graphics concept that changes what viewers see as they move around it.
sections: Created around Ahmedabad’s Conflictorium Museum, the installation explores diverse perspectives. It was designed for a Constitution Day exhibition at GMDC ground, with potential applications in museum corridors or on walls.

From one viewpoint, the panels present an illustration of what Conflictorium represents. From another, words communicate its essence. The viewer’s movement becomes the interaction that connects these two expressions.
outcome: An illustrated installation concept and physical mockup demonstrating how alternating viewpoints can change the message a visitor encounters.

name: An invitation with AR
label: Augmented reality · Experience design
headline: An invitation that opens into an experience.
description: A printed wedding invitation connects guests to location, outfit guidance, occasion dates, and a gallery.
scope: Printed invitation, AR content, guest information
sections: The invitation concept uses a smartphone or tablet scan to bring additional wedding information into an interactive experience. The printed card is the entry point into a broader set of guest touchpoints.

The proposed experience brings together location information, outfit guidance, occasion dates, and a photo gallery. These features address the practical questions guests may have before and during the celebration.
The location feature proposes map access and a three-dimensional view to help guests become familiar with the venue. It connects the invitation to the practical task of planning a visit.
outcome: An AR invitation concept linking print to interactive guest information. The project illustrates the proposed features; the website presents the case study rather than running the original AR experience.

name: Words with presence
label: Typography · Visual exploration
headline: When the arrangement becomes the message.
description: Typographic compositions exploring emphasis, contrast, and the visual rhythm of quotations.
sections: These compositions explore the relationship between words and their visual presentation. Changes in scale, position, and emphasis guide attention through each quotation.
A different voice for each composition
The second layout combines tightly arranged type with a contrasting final word. Each composition treats typography as the central visual material.
outcome: A pair of typographic explorations focused on emphasis, clarity, and expressive composition.

name: SIGnature · Arizona Science Center
label: UX research · Usability evaluation · Team project
headline: Making a science-center visit easier to plan.
description: A mixed-method UX evaluation translating visitor friction into clearer navigation, event discovery, and ticket-purchase flows.
scope: Heuristic evaluation · Survey · Moderated testing · UX recommendations
type: GIT 542 · With Stephan Bui and Idil Kale
sections: Before the visit comes the website.

Visitors need to answer practical questions quickly: what can I explore, what is happening on my visit date, and which tickets do I need? Team SIGnature examined where the Arizona Science Center website made those decisions difficult and translated the findings into prioritized design proposals.
Combining what people said with what they did.

Our team combined Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics, a WAVE accessibility review, 27 survey responses, and 9 moderated usability sessions conducted across three team members. The sequence moved from initial evaluation to survey insights, personas, task-based testing, synthesis, and recommendations.
Turning survey responses into research priorities.

My survey contribution included 15 respondents. Of these, 13 rated ticket purchasing as very important and 12 rated mobile compatibility as very important. Event discovery was less consistent: six found it easy, while six reported difficulty. These responses helped focus the evaluation on practical visitor tasks rather than visual preferences alone.

The study used three task-oriented personas: Alex, the efficient planner buying tickets; Maya, the event explorer checking what is on; and Jordan, the curious learner browsing exhibits. The test materials included three scenarios with three tasks each, think-aloud observation, and pre- and post-test questionnaires. This connected navigation decisions to concrete visitor goals.
The friction was in the journey, not one isolated page.

Across the evaluation, navigation labels and overlapping headers made orientation harder; the ticket journey lost context when it moved to an external system; event dates were difficult to surface; and text-heavy exhibit content was hard to scan. Affinity grouping and triangulation connected these observations to recurring problems and informed the recommendation priorities.
Give visitors a clear starting point.

The proposed homepage consolidates the header, uses clearer labels such as “Exhibits,” and gives Events a dedicated entry point. Hours, location, and Buy Tickets become easier to find. A consistent card grid and a better-positioned popup reduce competing demands on attention. Navigation and ticketing were treated as high-priority changes because they affect essential planning tasks.
Keep the purchase path visible from start to finish.

The proposed sequence is Date → Ticket Type → Add-ons → Review → Checkout. A persistent cart preserves context, while clearer grouping distinguishes required general admission from optional DOME or planetarium experiences. Earlier member sign-in helps visitors understand the relevant options before committing to a purchase.
Make “what’s on?” answerable at a glance.

The event direction places dates and times directly on cards and brings a “Today” entry point to the homepage. Filters by date, event type, and age help visitors narrow the list without opening every event. This proposal responds to the uneven event-discovery experience found in the survey and observed during evaluation.
Carry the same clarity onto a smaller screen.

The recommendations call for consistent behavior at a 375px mobile width, clearer visual hierarchy, and more scannable exhibit cards. Image compression and lazy loading support performance. The accessibility review informed the evaluation; these proposals would still need implementation checks and assistive-technology testing before claiming conformance.
The next question is whether the changes help.

This was a team research and recommendation project with Stephan Bui and Idil Kale, not a launched redesign. A follow-up study should include more parents, educators, and tourists; test the mobile prototypes; and capture consistent task completion, time on task, and perceived ease. Ticket and event flows would be the first priorities for validating the proposed changes.
outcome: Six prioritized recommendation areas connect research evidence to proposed design changes: ticketing, navigation, event discovery, homepage hierarchy, mobile usability, and exhibit browsing. The deliverable is an evidence-informed UX direction and prototype set; post-redesign improvements have not yet been measured.

name: Pra wellness identity
label: Logo design · Wellness branding
headline: A visual identity for a moment of calm.
description: A flowing wordmark and seven-color motif for a yoga and wellness center.
scope: Concept exploration, wordmark, typography, brand applications
sections: Create a sense of calm and personal growth
Pra is presented as a meditation and yoga wellness center, with an audience primarily aged 30–45. The identity explores an alternative to the conventional yoga-pose logo.
Find the idea behind the mark
The sketches explored letterforms, movement, and circular motifs. The final direction combines a flowing wordmark with seven colored dots that reference chakra symbolism within the design concept.
Flow, color, and a welcoming character
The wordmark uses customized Kalam lettering, paired with Gabriola for the tagline. Increasing dot sizes express growth and progress, while the colors communicate a sense of diversity and balance.
Carry the identity into everyday touchpoints
The concept extends into a yoga-mat mockup and an event flyer, exploring how the mark works across a product surface and a promotional layout.
outcome: A wellness identity concept with logo explorations, typography choices, and brand-application mockups.

name: Form, Function & Revolution
label: Research-led editorial · Typography
headline: Translating design history into a visual system.
description: An editorial exploration of El Lissitzky, geometric abstraction, and contemporary visual communication.
scope: Research synthesis, grid, cover iterations, typography, spreads
sections: Let the research shape the visual language

Form, Function, and Revolution examines El Lissitzky’s influence on visual communication. The publication responds to the geometric language and structural thinking of his work through a contemporary editorial system.
Explore different ways into the story
Cover and spread iterations tested changes in scale, white space, image placement, and text structure. Critique feedback helped refine dense sections and improve the rhythm of the pages.

Red, black, and light neutral areas provide contrast, while geometric forms and distinctive typography connect the pages. The final direction moves between expressive spreads and quieter text-led layouts.
Grid structure, typographic hierarchy, and recurring visual motifs organize the research into a cohesive sequence. Artworks are presented as part of the publication’s historical subject matter.
outcome: A research-informed editorial system and finished publication. The project strengthened grid design, typographic rhythm, and visual storytelling, with interactive adaptation identified as a possible next step.

name: ABPAL · Corporate & Product Catalog
label: Editorial design · B2B · Catalog
headline: A broad product range, brought into one clear catalog.
description: A 67-page corporate and product catalog connecting ABPAL’s company story, brands, product ranges, and service information.
sections: Structure for a wide range of information.

The catalog moves from the company overview and brand directory into product categories, specifications, infrastructure, and service information. Section openings and a consistent hierarchy help readers move between the company story and detailed product content.
Make technical information easy to scan.

Product photography, grouped specifications, contrasting headings, and repeating page structures bring consistency to a varied range. The selected pages below show the finished publication across corporate, product, and service content.
outcome: The finished publication brings ABPAL’s company overview, brand directory, product categories, specifications, and service information into one 67-page catalog. A consistent editorial hierarchy gives sales and product communication a shared reference. This is a delivered publication count, not a measured sales or conversion result.
